newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany appears happy with weak mark - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Germany appears happy with weak mark - analysts.

text.p: Germany's half-hearted verbal support of the mark this week has created the impression Bonn can live with a weak currency but would prefer foreign exchange markets to be less choppy, analysts said on Thursday.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's cabinet issued a bland statement on Wednesday saying recent sharp falls in the deutschemark against the U.S. dollar and sterling should not be dramatised.

The moves, the statement added, reflected fundamentals as well as speculation ahead of European economic and monetary union (EMU). But, beyond consulting with partner countries, no concrete action to prop up the mark was threatened.
"As far as verbal intervention is concerned, it was of a very low-decibel variety," Neil MacKinnon, chief economist at Citibank in London, told Reuters.

Currency strategists expect to hear more of the same when Kohl holds his traditional summer news conference on Friday -- his last appearance before the Bonn press before his summer vacation in the Austrian Alps.
Kohl is likely to repeat typical statements made by German leaders recently -- that the euro will be as strong as the mark, and that EMU will start on time, they say.
Government sources, loath to upset forex markets, told Reuters the current weakness of the mark increased the need to ensure that the euro is a solid currency.
The sources also said that worries that the euro might be weak were causing an overreaction on forex markets as investors shift funds into "Anglo-Saxon" currencies.

But, the analysts said, official statements do little to hide the fact that the sputtering German economy -- hit by record post-war unemployment and slack domestic demand -- is unable to sustain the mark's traditional strength.

"My read is that the German economy cannot live with a strong mark. Recovery to date has been exclusively dependent on exports -- largely courtesy of the weak mark over the past two years," MacKinnon said.
Analysts see no likelihood of the Bundesbank stepping in to raise interest rates as long as the mark steadies near six-year lows just below 1.80 to the dollar.

That view was backed by Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp, who said in an interview published on Thursday that the mark's correction was over and that recent foreign exchange market moves had been "unspectacular".
In the interview, held on Tuesday with Wirtschaftswoche magazine, Krupp also said that the Bundesbank's monetary policy could not be used to steer foreign exchange markets.
"It was always the declared policy of the Bundesbank, that monetary policy in an anchor currency country cannot be used to exercise exchange rate policy and to influence exchange rates," Krupp said.

Krupp declined direct comment on the likely outcome of the Bundesbank's next council meeting on July 24. "But one must see rationally; the domestic economy does not at present give any reason to alter interest rates," he said.

Some currency strategists said that Bonn and Frankfurt's passive position could encourage more dollar buying in a market which still likes the greenback thanks to its higher yield, its status as a save haven from EMU, and the strong U.S. economy.

"It does indicate that Germany is not committed to maintaining a strong mark," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago. "The Bundesbank may not like a weak mark, but there is little they can do about it at the moment."

MacKinnon agreed: "Investors are happy to push the dollar up to the 1.80 level, but increasingly currency economists and investors feel there is little impediment at this level. The market is talking about 1.90 or even two."
Don Smith, chief economist at HSBC Markets in London, said that, although the German authorities were relaxed for now on the mark, scope for more short-term dollar gains was limited.

"The message that we are getting is that they are more concerned about volatility than about the absolute level," Smith told Reuters. "We don't see it this weak by the year-end. We're moving towards levels where the DM looks cheap."

Smith said he was surprised by rumours of central bank intervention, which pushed up the mark on Thursday, but said that if there was a rapid fall in the currency the Bundesbank might take action to buy marks.

"If we see a clear break to 1.82 over the next few days, it is likely that the Bundesbank would try to turn it around through some sort of intervention," Smith said. A more dramatic move towards 1.90 might require a rate hike, he added.
